transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-12-09 16:00 PST
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Luis (Aventine CTO), Priya (Lead ML), Samir (Infra)

Summary: quick discovery focused on which path Aventine should take to go from prototype to production. They emphasized PII, compliance, and latency. Redwood outlined quickstart credits and how hosted can get them TTFT very quickly, while Dedicated/Private addresses isolation.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, I'm Maya at Redwood, and Jonah's our SE, we're excited to learn about what you're building at Aventine.
[00:09] Luis Ortega: Yeah thanks Maya, we— I'll give a quick context. We're building a clinical intake assistant, it touches PHI-ish data, so privacy's top concern. We want to prototype quickly but also need to plan for a production path if things look good.
[00:23] Maya Patel: Totally makes sense, quick question, are you already running any LLMs in prod or is this fresh?
[00:28] Priya Menon: Fresh, we've experimented with open-source checkpoints locally, a lot of toy tests. For the pilot we want to integrate via API and evaluate both latency and hallucination rates against our prompt set.
[00:39] Jonah Reed: Okay great, two threads then — fast time-to-first-token and then longer term hosting/privacy. For TTFT we generally mean from first request to usable streaming token output, which on hosted we can usually get under ~200-400ms for many models depending on sequence length.
[00:53] Samir Kapoor: Sorry quick interject — what's the difference between hosted with VPC peering versus a fully private on-prem? We're trying to understand network isolation in case it's required for compliance.
[01:03] Maya Patel: Good callout. Hosted (Redwood public API) is the fastest to get started: self-serve credits, minimal infra. VPC-hosted means private control plane + network peering into your VPC — we offer that as part of Private deployments. On-prem is our packaged option if you need air-gapped. Dedicated is in-between: reserved GPU pools for throughput and isolation but still managed by Redwood.
[01:23] Luis Ortega: Got it. For compliance, auditors want KMS control of keys, audit logs, and ideally no customer-identifiable data leaving our VPC. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS and audit log retention?
[01:36] Jonah Reed: Yes, we support KMS integrations and exportable audit logs. For private/VPC deployments you can bring your own KMS/HSM and we can configure retention to meet your policy. On hosted we have encryption at rest & transit and a managed KMS, we can discuss DPA terms.
[01:50] Priya Menon: About cost and latency tradeoffs — if we go hosted for the pilot, will the metrics be representative of what we'd see on dedicated? We need to understand whether we'll be validating the right performance profile.
[02:03] Jonah Reed: It's a common question. Hosted is helpful for functional validation and TTFT checks. Dedicated gives more predictable latency and throughput: dedicated GPUs with reserved capacity reduce variance on tail latency. If you expect to push to 50–100 qps steady, Dedicated is the safer production match. We also have quantization and kernel selection options that vary by deployment.
[02:23] Luis Ortega: For the pilot scope thinking 100k tokens/week, peak bursts ~40 qps, 95th percentile latency target ~300ms for short prompts. Is that realistic?
[02:34] Maya Patel: Yes that's within the typical pilot envelope. We'll provide a benchmark run to validate.
[02:38] Samir Kapoor: What about data retention — do you store inputs or outputs on the hosted tier? We need to ensure no retention by default.
[02:46] Jonah Reed: By default hosted keeps short-term logs for debugging but we have options to disable retention and opt-out of data collection. For enterprise plans we can enforce no retention and audit configurations.
[02:57] Priya Menon: Cool. Can you outline the quickstart path? How fast could we go from signup to first useful inference?
[03:05] Maya Patel: Absolutely — with our PLG/self-serve flow: signup, free credits, API keys, a one-page quickstart and example repo. Typical teams see their first streaming token in under an hour — TTFT for first request depends on network and model but the dev experience is optimized for immediate feedback. We'll also send a minimal curl and a streaming SDK example.
[03:28] Luis Ortega: Sounds promising. One followup: we have to run a benchmark that includes our prompts and real doc context. Can Redwood run a joint benchmark or do we run locally?
[03:39] Jonah Reed: We can do both. SE-led benchmark sessions are common — Jonah: we bring a test harness and run your prompt set against hosted and a dedicated config, capture latency, token cost, and quality metrics. We usually run a short synthetic load plus real prompt traces.
[03:53] Priya Menon: Perfect. Also curious about model variants and rollback — if we test a quantized model for cost savings, what's the regression safety?
[04:02] Jonah Reed: We provide model versioning and rollout controls — canary deploys and automatic fallback to a higher-fidelity variant if quality drops. Redwood Optimize tools recommend quantization profiles per workload but you'd validate on your prompt set.
[04:17] Luis Ortega: Nice. For the auditors, can you share SOC2 docs and any third-party penetration testing results?
[04:24] Maya Patel: Yes, we'll include SOC2 report and our security whitepaper with the KMS/HSM details. We'll also point to our compliance page and can set an NDA if needed.
[04:33] Samir Kapoor: About network topology — if we go VPC, what's the egress pattern? Do we need to open specific ports?
[04:39] Jonah Reed: For VPC peering it's mainly outbound HTTPS to the Redwood control endpoints; for private we can work with your infra to define egress rules. We'll share a network runbook.
[04:48] Priya Menon: Any gotchas with streaming and token-level billing we should watch for? We sometimes see retries causing duplicate tokens and skewing costs.
[04:58] Jonah Reed: Good point. We recommend idempotency keys on requests and client-side dedup. Our SDKs set up streaming reconnect behavior and we'll share best practices. Token-level cost can be broken down in the Console for per-route tracking.
[05:12] Luis Ortega: Timeline-wise, we want a pilot in January. We need to finish procurement and security signoffs by late December. Is that feasible?
[05:20] Maya Patel: Feasible. We'll prioritize security docs this week and set up the benchmark the week of the 20th. Credits can be provisioned immediately once you sign-up.
[05:29] Priya Menon: Awesome. Can you also share estimates for Dedicated monthly commit to hit our 40 qps burst? We want a ballpark to take to finance.
[05:36] Maya Patel: Sure — I'll include a ranges matrix: pay-as-you-go hosted, reserved Dedicated monthly tiers, and an enterprise on-prem letter-of-intent price range.
[05:46] Samir Kapoor: One more thing — do you support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning?
[05:49] Jonah Reed: Yes SSO via SAML/OIDC and SCIM for user provisioning are supported on the enterprise console.
[05:55] Luis Ortega: Great. This has been super useful.
[05:58] Maya Patel: Quick recap — we'll send SOC2/security docs, pricing ranges, a benchmark plan and a small example repo to get TTFT. We'll aim to have all that by Friday. Jonah will own the SE benchmark follow-up.
[06:11] Priya Menon: Thanks, looking forward.
[06:13] Jonah Reed: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

End of transcript.
